title: Practice: Red Shift and the Expanding Universe

questions.stem: An astronomer observes light from a distant galaxy and finds that the spectral lines are shifted towards the red end of the spectrum compared to the same lines measured in a laboratory. What does this indicate?

options.text: The galaxy is moving towards us
The galaxy is moving away from us
The galaxy is not moving
The galaxy is hotter than expected

questions.explanation: Red shift occurs when the wavelength of light is stretched (shifted towards the red, longer-wavelength end of the spectrum). This happens when the source is moving away from the observer. If the galaxy were moving towards us (A), we would observe blue shift (shorter wavelengths). Red shift is not related to temperature (D). This is analogous to the Doppler effect with sound -- an ambulance siren drops in pitch as it moves away.

questions.stem: Hubble observed that more distant galaxies have greater red shifts. According to Hubble's law (v = H0 x d), if galaxy A is twice as far away as galaxy B, how does galaxy A's recession speed compare to galaxy B's?

options.text: Galaxy A moves at the same speed as galaxy B
Galaxy A moves at half the speed of galaxy B
Galaxy A moves at twice the speed of galaxy B
Galaxy A moves at four times the speed of galaxy B

questions.explanation: Hubble's law states v = H0 x d, where v is the recession velocity, H0 is the Hubble constant, and d is the distance. The relationship is directly proportional: if distance doubles, velocity doubles. Galaxy A at twice the distance moves at twice the speed. This was Hubble's key discovery -- the universe is expanding, and the expansion rate is proportional to distance. Option D would imply a squared relationship, which is not what Hubble's law describes.

questions.stem: If all distant galaxies are moving away from us, does this mean Earth is at the centre of the universe?

options.text: Yes, because all galaxies are moving away from Earth
No -- the expansion has no centre. Every point in the universe sees all other points moving away, like dots on an inflating balloon
Yes, because the Big Bang started at Earth's location
No, because only some galaxies are moving away

questions.explanation: The expansion of the universe has no centre. An observer anywhere in the universe would see all distant galaxies receding. A common analogy is dots drawn on a balloon -- as the balloon inflates, every dot sees every other dot moving away, but no dot is at the 'centre' of the expansion. The Big Bang did not happen at a specific point in space (C) -- it was an expansion of space itself. All distant galaxies show red shift, not just some (D).

questions.stem: A galaxy has a recession velocity of 15,000 km/s. The Hubble constant H0 is approximately 70 km/s/Mpc. Using Hubble's law, approximately how far away is this galaxy?

options.text: About 21 Mpc
About 214 Mpc
About 1,050,000 Mpc
About 0.0047 Mpc

questions.explanation: Using v = H0 x d, rearranged to d = v / H0 = 15,000 / 70 = 214.3 Mpc (megaparsecs). Option A divides incorrectly. Option C multiplies instead of dividing. Option D inverts the calculation. One megaparsec is approximately 3.26 million light years, so this galaxy is about 700 million light years away.

questions.stem: Red shift provides evidence that the universe is expanding. Which additional observation supports the Big Bang theory?

options.text: The Sun rises in the east every day
The cosmic microwave background radiation -- a faint glow of microwave radiation coming from all directions in space
The Moon orbits the Earth
Stars appear to twinkle at night

questions.explanation: The cosmic microwave background (CMB) radiation is the remnant heat from the early, hot universe, cooled by the expansion to microwave wavelengths. It was predicted by the Big Bang theory and discovered in 1965 by Penzias and Wilson. It comes from all directions uniformly, which is consistent with the entire universe once being extremely hot and dense. The other options (A, C, D) are unrelated to the origin of the universe.
